Q: Setting up and using Meld as your git difftool and mergetool on a Mac A:

From Mac OS High Sierra (10.13.6), Git 2.12.2

Install Meld

brew tap homebrew/cask

brew cask install meld

  • or brew install meld for newer versions of brew

Set Meld as Git Mergetool

git config --global merge.tool meld

git config --global diff.guitool meld

Q: Replica DR drills A:

I'll describe how we did failover at my last job. We used MySQL, not PostgreSQL, but the principles are the same. I won't mention specific commands though.

The first suggestion is to make failover a routine, not just something you do for drills. We had many replica sets, and we did failovers daily. We did this in response to issues like server failure, but we also did it during upgrades of the database or the OS (which were required), or even when reconfiguring database server startup options.

By making failover something you do regularly your whole team gets more practice with the procedure. If anything changes in your infrastructure that could interfere with the failover process, you know immediately that you need to fix it. You don't want to learn about that kind of issue only during the emergency.

We developed scripts to execute the failover. Then later we upgraded the scripts to a robust microservice written in Go, which could execute a failover for any named replica set, with lots of defensive code to catch errors and roll back safely, log the event, notify people who need to know, and so on.

Here's the sequence of steps we used:

  1. Kill client connections on the primary database and the replica. If any app try to reconnect, kill their connections too. Keep doing that in a loop until the failover is complete (see below).
  2. Set the primary to read-only mode.
  3. Wait for asynchronous replication to finish applying on the replica. This should only take a second. If the replica was lagging behind, it's not a good time to do a failover. AFAIK, if you use PostgreSQL synchronous replication, this step may not be needed, because there should never be replication lag.
  4. Reconfigure the direction of replication if necessary. In MySQL, it was easy to just configure the primary and replica with bidirectional replication, so this step was not necessary. I haven't used bidirectional replication on PostgreSQL. I've read that an extension is needed if you want to do that, but I don't have experience so I can't recommend one.
  5. Change the virtual IP address apps use to connect to the primary database. We used BGP to move an IP address from one instance to the other. This was very fast—less than 1 second. You could also do this with DNS, but that's bound to be slower.
  6. Set the new primary (formerly the replica) to read-write mode.
  7. Apps may now be allowed to connect via the virtual IP to the new primary. Stop the loop that has been killing client connections.

The killing of client connections is necessary, because it's important to avoid conflicting updates.

By using a virtual IP (or DNS name), the apps don't need to be reconfigured during failover. They just connect to the same endpoint they already know about.

We could do failover any time, even during peak hours, and the applications using databases experienced only a brief disconnection. Apps must be coded to handle disconnections gracefully, by reconnecting automatically.

Q: Ocaml: weighted graph A:

First of all let me define the model of you graph, so that we can speak the same language. You're using a edge list to represent a graph. For a graph of type 'a graph we will say that 'a is node, and 'a * 'a = node * node is an edge. So the graph itself is represented as edge list. To represent a weighted graph you're using edges that are labeled with weights, so the edge has now type node * weight * node, where weight has type int.

Now, let's go to your problem. If you look carefully in bfs implementation you will notice, that visited has type node list (i.e., int list), not edge list. And you're applying your predicate to a value of type node, not to an edge. The same should be true to your bfs_w function. But here you, for some reason, decided that you're storing edges in a visited list, and used you own find function, instead of List.mem that is fully applicable here. 

let bfs_w graph_w p start =
  let rec search visited = function
    | [] -> raise Not_found
    | n :: rest ->
      if List.mem n visited
      then search visited rest
      else if p n then n
      else search (n::visited) (rest @ (succ_w graph_w n)) in
  search [] [start]

This implementation will have a correct type, expecting a user predicate that accepts a value of type node.

Q: MongoError: connect ECONNREFUSED 127.0.0.1:27017 A:

I was having the same problem today... And I had been searching for answers. I am on Ubuntu. However, I could not find the correct one that works in answers to this question. After much research, the following worked for me finally!! :)

First, after running

mongod dbpath

if appeared that MongoDB was looking for the data/db directory, which was missing in my installed MongoDB application, so I ran the following commands:

sudo mkdir -p /data/db

Then run

sudo chown -R $USER /data/db

chown - changes ownership of files/directories. I.e., owner of the file/directory changes to the specified one, but it doesn't modify permissions. As detailed on How are chown and chmod command different in the given operation?.

Finally, run

sudo systemctl enable mongod.service

It will give a message: I created symbolic link /etc/systemd/system/multi-user.target.wants/mongod.service → /lib/systemd/system/mongod.service and started the service.
